title: Turn it and turn it (Avot 5:22)
hookLine: Ben Bag Bag: turn it and turn it, for everything is in it
tomorrow: opening night's done. was the work worth it either way?

cards: A comfort show, watched for the fifth time, and suddenly a joke you never caught. A song on repeat that lands differently the week everything changes. Same words, new thing.
So why read the same old text again and again? Ben Bag Bag, a sage in Avot with a name like a drumbeat, answers with a verb you can do with your hands.

teach.h: TURN IT, AND TURN IT AGAIN.
teach.b: Ben Bag Bag says of the Torah: turn it and turn it, for everything is in it. Look into it. Grow gray and old over it.
Don't move from it, for you have no better portion than it. Turn it: the way you turn a stone in your hand to see the side that was facing down.
The text stays the same. The light changes, and so do you. A line read young and read again with gray hair is the same ink and a different reading.
You've already watched this happen on this path. A few days ago, the ten sayings. Someone turned Genesis one, counted the and God saids, and found only nine.

teach.h: THE TENTH SAYING, FOUND BY TURNING.
teach.b: The Talmud turned it again and found the tenth hiding in the first words: in the beginning. Nobody added a word. Someone just turned it one more time.
Notice the end of the saying, too.
Grow gray over it. Ben Bag Bag doesn't picture a finish line. He pictures a reader who keeps coming back, until the hair changes color and the text still hasn't run out.
Everything is in it is less a claim you can check in an afternoon than an invitation to try: turn it, turn it, and see.

how: In Jewish study the same texts are read again every year: the Torah is read through in a yearly cycle in the synagogue, and learners return to the same pages of Mishnah and Talmud, often with a study partner.

games.q: what does “turn it and turn it” mean?
o: reading the same text again and again
turning the page to start a new book
flipping a coin to settle a question

games.q: Ben Bag Bag's saying — tap the pairs.
p: read again, from a new side

s: 'turn it and turn it' means flip to a new text
it means turn the same Torah over and over: everything is in it.
Ben Bag Bag says to grow gray and old over it
he pictures a reader who never finishes, and a text that never runs out.

games.q: your book club wants to reread last year's pick. one member groans: 'we already did that one.' what would Ben Bag Bag say?
o: turn it again: a second reading shows what the first one missed.
skip it; turning means moving on to a fresh book each time.
read just the summary, since everything was already in the first read.
games.why: turn it and turn it, for everything is in it. the same text, read again, isn't the same reading.

practice: Take one short line you know by heart: a verse, a saying from this path, even a lyric. Say it out loud slowly, three times, leaning on a different word each time, and listen to how the meaning tilts.
For the rest of the sit, keep turning it silently.

wordCard.voice: Turn it and turn it: Ben Bag Bag's advice for the Torah. The same text, read again, from a new side.

orig.note: Hebrew: turn it and turn it (Avot 5:22).

carryVoice: One to hold: turn it, turn it, because everything is in it and nothing runs out. See you tomorrow.
